title: Latency-Fidelity Lanes — Personal Brainlog
content:
Context:
This is a personal scratchpad for an idea that keeps bubbling up in support and Solutions: expose explicit latency/fidelity "lanes" on the Redwood API so product teams can pick or auto-adapt to a guaranteed latency envelope with associated quality and price.

Why this?
- Customers repeatedly ask for deterministic perceptual latency (p95) guarantees per route.
- Current levers (batching, model choice, quantization) are powerful but invisible to app developers.
- A lane abstraction could make tradeoffs explicit and enable automated adaptation per session or user segment.

Problem statement (short):
Apps want predictable latency bounds without manually juggling models, quant profiles, and batching. We need an ergonomic runtime-level primitive: Latency-Fidelity Lanes.

Goals / success signals:
- Developer ergonomics: <5 minute setup to attach a lane to an existing route.
- Observable: clear per-lane p50/p95/p99 and per-token cost.
- Adaptive savings: reduce median token cost by >=15% for non-critical traffic via automated lane downshifts while keeping user satisfaction >95% in evals.

Constraints / non-goals:
- Not replacing full model pinning or dedicated capacity. Lanes are a routing/contract primitive layered above model variants.
- We won't invent new quant formats; lanes map to existing model variants + runtime config.
- Initial launch limited to hosted + dedicated (no VPC private on day1).

Concept sketch:
1) Lane definitions (config):
   - lane_id: string (e.g., "fast-10ms", "balanced-200ms", "high-fidelity-1s")
   - target_p95_ms: integer
   - allowed_models: list of compatible model families/variants (gpt-mini, gpt-medium-q4, gpt-xl)
   - max_tokens_per_call: integer (soft limit to keep latency predictable)
   - fallback_policy: ordered list (downshift, queue, offload-to-sync)
   - cost_multiplier: float (for pricing UI and cost attribution)
   - preemptible: boolean (if true, lane may be preempted in overload)

2) Runtime enforcement:
   - Router assigns request to lane by route config / request header / per-user mapping.
   - Serving runtime enforces a per-request decoding budget tied to lane, with early-abort or partial result behavior if budget exceeded.
   - KV-prefix caching prioritized by lane (fast lanes use hot-cache paths).

3) Adaptive lane switching:
   - Session-level: start in the lane configured by user segment. If response length or model time predicts breach, the runtime can switch mid-response using a two-pass strategy: cheap model for draft-> expensive for refinement (or vice versa).
   - Granularity: per-request, per-session, or per-token (experimental).

API and UX sketch (developer-facing):
- New param on generation endpoints: lane=string or lane_policy={segment:..., fallback:...}
- Console: visualize lane p95, model mix, and cost per 1k tokens. Quick toggle to preview lane quality via sample prompt.

User stories (prioritized):
- As a product engineer, I can set route default lane to "balanced-200ms" so my chat replies hit 200ms p95 without touching model config.
- As a customer success engineer, I can propose a lane to a customer and show 3-month savings projection.
- As an SRE, I can mark a lane preemptible and have runtime evict it under spare capacity pressure.
- As an API user, I can request lane=fast for a particular request to get quicker but possibly lower-fidelity results.

Acceptance criteria (MVP):
- Route-level lane config accepted by API/Console.
- Runtime enforces a latency budget for 95% of calls in synthetic load tests.
- Metrics pipeline tracks lane->model mapping and cost attribution.
- Quickstart doc and example app updated.

Experiment ideas and evals:
- AB test: balanced lane vs unconstrained baseline measuring task success on a subset of LLM evals (QA, summarization, dialogue).
- User-facing quality guardrails: for downshifted responses, run lightweight reranker in fast lane to avoid catastrophic failures.
- Simulate mid-response switch: generate with small model for first pass then run refinement on tail tokens; measure latency and quality delta.

Observability and metrics to ship first:
- lane.request.count, lane.request.latency.p50/p95/p99, lane.token.cost, lane.model.mix%, lane.fallback.count
- Per-route user satisfaction proxy: reranker-score or closed-form eval on sample prompts

Pricing implications (notes):
- We can expose cost_multiplier in billing UI. Example: fast lane = 0.6x cost, balanced = 1.0x, high-fidelity = 1.8x (reflects model mix and kernel cost).
- Must ensure transparency: show customers the model mix and sample responses used in cost calc.

Rollout plan (high-level):
- Phase 0 (prototypes): internal dogfood + experiments on prod traffic slice (3 weeks)
- Phase 1 (MVP public): console + API support for lanes, metrics, simple fallback (2 months)
- Phase 2: adaptive mid-response switching, finer-grained per-token adaptation, private/VPC support (Q2 after launch)

Open questions / risks:
- How to quantify "fidelity" across model families? Need better eval hooks that map to human judgement beyond perplexity.
- Billing complexity and disputes if cost multipliers misalign with perceived quality.
- Edge cases: long-form generation may be inherently incompatible with strict p95 targets. Need graceful error semantics.
- Security and compliance: can preemptible lanes be used in regulated workloads? probably not — need policy.

Short-term TODOs (for me):
- Draft a short PRD stub and route it to Miles and Tess for feedback (this doc -> INF-912).
- Prototype lane param in SDK shim (Node + Python) and run against local runtime harness.
- Define 10 sample prompts across domains to standardize lane evaluation.

Notes to self:
- Keep lane config small and composable. Start with 3 lanes: "fast", "balanced", "high".
- Focus on developer UX and observability first; complex auto-adapt can iterate later.
- Talk to pricing for a simple multiplier model, avoid per-token dynamic pricing on rollout.

End of brainlog.

(Fragments, TODOs and stream-of-consciousness above — save as draft, sync with INF-912 when ready.)
